fact_en: Earth's poles stay cold because slanted sunlight spreads thin, making the warmth weak. Plus, the white ice reflects most of that light right back into space!
fact_bis: Bugnaw ang mga polo sa Yuta kay hapdos ang kahayag sa adlaw ug mokatag, maong huyang ang init. Gipasanag pa balik sa puti nga yelo ang kadaghanan sa kahayag!

findings.note: BODY defect. EN: "poles stay cold because slanted sunlight spreads thin, making the warmth weak." BIS: "Bugnaw ang mga polo sa Yuta kay HAPDOS ang kahayag sa adlaw ug mokatag..." In Cebuano hapdos = stinging/smarting pain, not slanted (hilig / pahilig). The card therefore says polar sunlight is STINGING and nothing in the card ever restores the slant — the whole causal mechanism (light arrives at an angle, so it spreads thin) is gone, replaced by a claim that contradicts the 'huyang ang init' conclusion. title_bis "Hilis Sikat Polo" is also Tagalog (hilis/sikat), so no correct word appears anywhere on the card.

fact_en: A total solar eclipse happens because the Sun and Moon look almost the same size from Earth, even though the Sun is actually much bigger!
fact_bis: Mahitabo ang total solar eclipse kay halos magkasinglaki ang Adlaw ug Bulan gikan sa Kalibutan, bisan og mas dako gyud ang Adlaw!

findings.note: title_bis "Adlaw ug Bulan Laki" for "Sun & Moon Same Size": in Cebuano laki = MALE (Tagalog laki = size/bigness), so the title reads "Sun and Moon Male" and the whole point of the card — that the two LOOK almost the same size from Earth — is gone from the title. The body repeats the same Tagalogism ("halos magkasinglaki ang Adlaw ug Bulan") instead of the Cebuano gidak-on/kasingkadako, so the card never states the equal-apparent-size fact in correct Cebuano; all that survives is "bisan og mas dako gyud ang Adlaw" (the Sun is really bigger), which alone does not answer why a total solar eclipse can happen. Corpus confirms the reading: the same corpus uses "Laki nga Putyukan" for drone (male) bees and "Laki nga Lamok" for male mosquito, and uses gidak-on 349x / kasingkadako for size against only 3 uses of kasinglaki.

fact_en:
Why are intensity reports so important after an earthquake?

They show which places were shaken the hardest! This helps responders know exactly where to send help and rescue.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga importante ang mga ulat sa intensity human sa linog?

Nagpakita kini kon asa pinakakusog ang pag-uyog! Makatabang kini sa mga responder kon asa magpadala ug tabang ug rescue.

findings.note: bis question "Ngano nga importante ang mga ulat sa intensity human sa linog?" — Cebuano ulat = SCAR (a healed-wound mark); the Tagalog ulat = report does not carry over. The card therefore asks about earthquake "scars" rather than PHIVOLCS intensity REPORTS, and no Cebuano sentence in the card ever names a report (taho/report); the answer sentences ("Nagpakita kini... Makatabang kini sa mga responder") just inherit the wrong referent, so a child learns that damage marks — not the reported intensity data — are what direct rescuers. Corpus confirms the sense: the only other corpus title using the word is "Ulat sa Hilum" = "Hilum Attachment Scar".

fact_en:
What are the natural warning signs of a tsunami?

If you feel a strong earthquake at the coast or hear a loud roar from the sea, a tsunami may be coming!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang natural nga timailhan sa tsunami?

Kon mabati nimo ang kusog nga linog sa baybayon o madunggan ang kusog nga dahunog gikan sa dagat, tingali tsunami na ang moabot!

findings.note: title_bis "Natural nga Babag" = "natural OBSTACLE/BARRIER" (babag = to block/obstruct), but the card is about natural WARNING SIGNS of a tsunami (title_en "Natural Warning Signs"). The body uses the correct word, "Unsa ang natural nga timailhan sa tsunami?" — so the title is the outlier and names a different thing. Same card's sibling (ffct-29278) correctly titles warning as "Babala", and the corpus uses babag correctly for real barriers elsewhere in this batch (ffct-29359 "Mga bukid ang mobabag sa hangin"). Corpus-wide seam: 11 other title_bis use Babag where title_en says warning (e.g. ffct-31425 "Tsunami Warnings"->"Babag sa Tsunami", ffct-30616 "Buoys Early Warning"->"Buoy Sensor Sayong Babag", ffct-32639 "Color-Coded Rain Warnings"->"Kolor nga Babag").

fact_en: Signal No. 4 means very strong, destructive storm winds may arrive within about 12 hours and can heavily damage many houses!
fact_bis: Ang Signal No. 4 nagpasabot nga adunay grabe ka kusog ug makaguba nga hangin nga moabot sulod sa mga 12 ka oras ug makaguba sa daghang balay!

findings.note: title_bis "Signal 4 sa Kapeckan" — same non-word as ffct-29335 standing in for danger/hazard (title_en "Signal Number 4"). Not Cebuano and not recoverable by a reader; body ("grabe ka kusog ug makaguba nga hangin... sulod sa mga 12 ka oras") is correct, so only the title is defective.

fact_en: PAGASA uses color-coded rainfall warnings: yellow means be aware, orange means be ready, and red means evacuate! These colors show how heavy the rain is and the flood danger.
fact_bis: Naggamit ang PAGASA og color-coded rainfall warnings: dalaw nagpasabot pag-amping, kahel nagpasabot pangandam, ug pula nagpasabot mobakwit! Gipakita niini kung unsa kakusog ang ulan ug ang peligro sa baha.

findings.note: "dalaw nagpasabot pag-amping, kahel nagpasabot pangandam, ug pula nagpasabot mobakwit" — YELLOW is rendered as "dalaw", which is not a colour word in Cebuano (yellow = dalag, or dilaw/dulaw; "dalaw" reads as Tagalog for a visit). The whole point of the card is the three-colour->three-action mapping, and the first pair is broken with no recovery anywhere in the card: a child cannot learn which rainfall warning colour means 'be aware'. Corpus uses dalag 232x and the parallel card ffct-29804 uses "dilaw, orange, ug pula"; this is the only "dalaw" colour hit in the whole corpus.

fact_en: Strong wind isn't the only danger! Heavy rain from typhoons causes floods and landslides, which often harm even more people.
fact_bis: Dili lang ang kusog nga hangin ang peligro! Ang kusog nga ulan sa bagyo maoy hinungdan sa baha ug landslide, nga kasagarang mas daghan pa ang madisgrasya.

findings.note: title_bis "Kapeckan sa Bagyo" for title_en "Typhoon Hazards Beyond Wind": "kapeckan" is not a Cebuano word (the 'ck' cluster does not occur in Cebuano orthography) and it is the only content word in the title, so the title says nothing — it does not resolve to kapeligrohan, katalagman or any guessable word. Never appears in any card body corpus-wide, only in 7 titles, so it is a generation artifact rather than regional usage. Body is fine and delivers the fact; the title is unreadable.

fact_en: Erosion is when heavy rain and strong wind wash away our rich and healthy topsoil!
fact_bis: Ang erosion mahitabo kung ang kusog nga ulan ug hangin maghanas sa tambok nga topsoil!

findings.note: "Ang erosion mahitabo kung ang kusog nga ulan ug hangin MAGHANAS sa tambok nga topsoil" — hanas/kahanas in Cebuano means SKILLED / practised (corpus uses it that way ~25 times: "hanas nga mangangayam", "Kahanas sa Observing"), not "wash away". The card is a single-sentence definition of erosion, so nothing restores the meaning: a child reads that rain and wind 'train/practise' the topsoil and never learns soil is carried off. The correct verbs are used elsewhere in this same batch (ffct-29403 "aron dili kini dali nga MAANOD"; ffct-29286 "makaBANLAS").

fact_en: The Sun doesn't disappear at night! The Earth simply turns around, making our side face away from it.
fact_bis: Wala mawala ang Adlaw sa gabii! Nagtuyok lang ang Yuta, busa ang atong bahin nag-atubang palayo niini.

findings.note: title_bis "Adlaw sa Gabii ug Tirok" for title_en "Night and Earth's Turning" — tirok means to gather/congregate in Cebuano, not to rotate; rotation is tuyok. The body uses the right word ("Nagtuyok lang ang Yuta"), so the title is the outlier and names a different concept than the card teaches.

fact_en: When the Sun runs out of hydrogen, it will swell up huge and become a giant red star called a red giant!
fact_bis: Kung mahurot na sa Adlaw ang hydrogen niini, mohabok kini ug mahimong dako nga pula nga bituon nga gitawag red giant!

findings.note: title_bis "Red Giant Uma" for title_en "Future Red Giant Sun" — "uma" is Cebuano for FARM/field (it is used correctly with that meaning in ffct-29528's title "Konstelasyon Uma" in this same batch). It appears to be a truncation of "umaabot" (future), leaving a star card labelled "Red Giant Farm".

fact_en: Not all rain flows in rivers! Some soaks into the ground, collecting as groundwater that we get from wells and springs.
fact_bis: Dili tanang ulan modagayday sa suba! Ang uban mosuhop sa yuta, matipon isip groundwater nga makuha nato sa atabay ug tuburan.

findings.note: title_bis "Groundwater sa Balon" — Tagalog false friend: balon is Tagalog for "well", but in Cebuano balon = provisions/food taken on a trip (a well is atabay or bubon). The card's own body uses the correct word ("makuha nato sa atabay ug tuburan"), which marks the title as the outlier; the title as written labels the card with a different thing entirely.

fact_en: It is rare for an animal to become a fossil! It must be buried quickly before it rots or is eaten by others.
fact_bis: Panagsa ra mahimong fossil ang usa ka mananap! Kinahanglan kini dali nga matabunan sa dili pa madunot o kan-on sa lain.

findings.note: title_bis "Lalim nga Mahimong Fossil" for "Fossils Are Rare". In Cebuano "lalim" means EASY (the everyday phrase "dili lalim" = not easy); read as Tagalog it means depth. Either way the title asserts the opposite of, or nothing about, rarity. The card's own body has it right ("Panagsa ra mahimong fossil"), and the corpus uses talagsaon/panagsa for rare elsewhere, so the title is the outlier. Same swap recurs in ffct-29065 ("Gems Are Rare" -> "Lalim nga mga Hiyas").
